openers.middle-triassic-epoch: A third extinction since the Permian closed the Early Triassic, yet what followed was a rebound. Within 4–6 million years of the Great Dying, complex ecosystems full of specialized animals began to re-form, as fossils such as China's Luoping biota record. Archosaurs pushed the therapsids aside to rule the land, while placodonts, Tanystropheus and other marine reptiles joined the ichthyosaurs at sea. Stony corals, the first stem turtles and the oldest sure lepidosaur all appear. Underneath it all, Pangaea began to crack: rift valleys opened soon after the Siberian Traps fell silent, and the Tethys pushed west.
openers.late-triassic-epoch: The Late Triassic opens with a crisis at sea and a shock to the climate. Marine reptiles had just suffered their highest extinction rates, and then the Wrangellia flood basalts poured out over about 5 million years, jolting global climate for perhaps 1–2 million years. In the rains and rivers of that world, the first true dinosaurs appeared and quickly split into sauropodomorphs and meat-eating theropods. Rift basins in Argentina and Virginia buried them with fish, insects and reptiles, while a vast delta plain spread across the Boreal Ocean. Even the oldest probable moth scales turn up, swallowed by a plant-eater.

reviews.middle-triassic-epoch: The Middle Triassic is the story of a world rebuilding. Some 4–6 million years after the extinction, carbon-isotope swings calmed and complex food webs returned, from coral-building seas to Chinese lakes with six or more trophic levels. Marine reptiles crowded the expanding Tethys, preserved in lagoons such as Monte San Giorgio, while archosaurs took over the land and the first flies, stem turtles and lepidosaurs appeared. At the same time the crust was moving: rifts opened along the future Atlantic, and Cimmerian blocks drifted north to close the Paleo-Tethys. A long cooling from 242 Ma held until the Wrangellia eruptions broke it.

tria-042.title: Dinoflagellates leave their first fossil cysts
tria-042.text: Chemical traces say dinoflagellates may have drifted in the sea since the Early Cambrian. Their first true fossils, though, appear only in the mid-Triassic, mostly as tough resting cysts. These single-celled plankton then radiated in shape from the Late Triassic through the Middle Jurassic. By then they had become prominent phytoplankton, the drifting algae of the open sea.

tria-044.title: Turtles start out without a shell
tria-044.text: The first turtles had no shell at all. Pappochelys, a stem turtle from the Middle Triassic, an early member of the turtle line, had only a short torso, broad ribs and long back vertebrae. By the Late Triassic, Odontochelys carried a complete bony plastron, the belly shell, but only part of a carapace, the upper shell. The traits that built the shell may first have helped these animals dig.

tria-046.title: Placodonts, nothosaurs and kin crowd Triassic seas
tria-046.text: Nothosaurs 5–7 m long hunted Middle Triassic waters, and they had plenty of company. Placodonts, thalattosaurs, the long-necked Tanystropheus and other marine reptiles joined the ichthyosaurs and sauropterygians. Pachypleurosaurs and nothosaurs were common, especially around the Tethys. Atopodentatus is the earliest known plant-eating marine reptile, and some ichthyopterygians reached very large body masses. South China has yielded almost every known clade, or branch, of Triassic marine reptile.

tria-047.title: Seas and lakes rebuild complex food webs
tria-047.text: Fossil dung from Chinese lakes tells the story. By the early Ladinian, these coprolites record freshwater food webs with six or more trophic levels, rungs from grazers up to top predators. Some 4–6 million years after the extinction, complex ecosystems full of specialized animals had begun to re-form. Carbon-isotope swings abruptly calmed, and the recovery of shelled sea life soon followed. Marine reptiles, ray-finned fishes, ammonoids, bivalves and gastropods all grew more diverse, crinoids regained ecological dominance, and phytoplankton, corals and crustaceans recovered. Even so, full recovery took about 30 million years. Global marine diversity regained its old level only in the Middle Jurassic.

tria-050.title: The Tethys pushes west and floods central Europe
tria-050.text: Central Europe went under the sea. In the Middle Triassic the Tethys, a vast gulf on Pangaea's eastern side, opened farther west as the older Paleo-Tethys shrank. Rising seas spread the shallow Muschelkalk Sea across central Europe, as far as the North Pyrenean Zone. Rifting also began in the Anisian to form a new ocean basin, the Meliata.

tria-051.title: France's Grès à Voltzia keeps the first aphids
tria-051.text: The oldest known aphids come from a sandstone in France. The Grès à Voltzia, about 245 million years old, is a Lagerstätte, a site of exceptional fossil preservation. Its varied arthropods also include finely detailed myriapods, the many-legged group of centipedes and millipedes.

tria-052.title: Agriodontosaurus, the oldest sure lepidosaur
tria-052.text: The family tree of every lizard and snake runs back to a small reptile from England. Agriodontosaurus, a rhynchocephalian about 244–241.5 million years old, is the oldest definite lepidosaur. Lepidosaurs are the ancestors of lizards, snakes and the tuatara. The next oldest rhynchocephalian, Wirtembergia, is Ladinian, and the Early Triassic Sophineta may be a lepidosaur relative. The group later diversified during {{ref:tria-066}}.

tria-054.title: Monte San Giorgio's lagoon preserves sea reptiles
tria-054.text: A stagnant lagoon made a perfect tomb. At Monte San Giorgio on Lake Lugano, a Middle Triassic lagoon sat behind reefs, and its oxygen-free bottom was ideal for fossilization. Its Besano Formation, about 242 million years old and now a World Heritage Site, preserves fish and marine reptiles such as Neusticosaurus and Tanystropheus.

tria-053.title: A long cooling settles over the Ladinian and Carnian
tria-053.text: After the Anisian chill, the world kept drifting cooler. The Ladinian–Carnian Cooling ran from 242 to 233 million years ago, and global temperatures were still relatively cool as the Carnian began. Then abrupt warming from the Wrangellia eruptions around 234 million years ago ended the trend.

tria-057.title: True flies take wing
tria-057.text: One wing, 10 mm long, from Mt. Crosby in Australia is unusually large for a Triassic fly. The first true flies, the Diptera, appeared in the Middle Triassic around 240 million years ago and spread widely through the Middle and Late Triassic. They form one of the four great insect radiations, evolutionary bursts. Many new species of lower flies arose around 220 million years ago.

tria-055.title: Cimmerian blocks drift north and close the Paleo-Tethys
tria-055.text: An ocean that had lasted about 400 million years was squeezed shut. A string of continental fragments, the Cimmerian blocks, drifted north, closing the Paleo-Tethys ahead of them and opening the Neo-Tethys behind. By the Late Triassic the old ocean had shrunk to a narrow seaway. Its closure raised the Cimmerian orogeny, which began about 240–200 million years ago as the blocks collided with Kazakhstania and North and South China. The Qiangtang terrane of northern Tibet joined Asia in the Late Triassic. The western arm stayed open until about 205 million years ago, when Iranian blocks hit Eurasia's Turan platform. The finished belt ran from Anatolia east to the Indosinian orogen.

tria-058.title: Marine reptiles suffer their steepest extinction rates
tria-058.text: For the sea reptiles of the Mesozoic, no moment was deadlier. At the end of the Ladinian, which closed the Middle Triassic, they suffered their highest extinction rates. Like fishes, marine reptiles lost much of their diversity between the Middle Triassic and the Jurassic.

tria-062.title: Specialist rhynchosaurs spread across the globe
tria-062.text: A crisis gave one narrow branch the whole world. Rhynchosaurs had diversified around 240 million years ago, but the lines common in the Middle Triassic died out during {{ref:tria-066}}. The specialized hyperodapedontines were left. They became widespread and abundant in the late Carnian, giving rhynchosaurs their broadest, truly global range.

tria-064.title: A giant delta plain fills the Boreal Ocean
tria-064.text: Rivers built new land across a whole sea floor. From 237 to 227 million years ago, a vast delta plain spread across northern Pangaea's Triassic Boreal Ocean, today's Barents Sea. Rapid sedimentation after the extinction had already built a shallow basin, with Induan silts spanning 1,000 km. Deposition slowed in the Olenekian and Anisian, then revived in the Ladinian, as deltas advanced more than 500 km. By 237 million years ago, the plain had formed.

tria-060.title: Chalk-plated coccolithophores join the plankton
tria-060.text: Since about 220 million years ago, the seafloor has never stopped collecting microscopic chalk plates. Calcareous nannofossils, those tiny chalky remains, have a continuous record from the Late Triassic to the present. The oldest known coccolithophores, algae armored with plates called coccoliths, date from around the Norian–Rhaetian boundary. One source puts the first coccoliths, with dinoflagellates, in the plankton earlier, during {{ref:tria-066}}. Coccolithophores radiated in the Early to Middle Jurassic, becoming prominent members of the phytoplankton.

tria-065.title: Moth scales turn up in fossil dung
tria-065.text: The oldest probable trace of moths was eaten by accident. Scales about 236 million years old, found in a plant-eater's dung in Argentina, are the earliest probable fossils of Lepidoptera, the moths and butterflies. Wing scales of several moth groups occur as rare microfossils at the Triassic–Jurassic boundary in a core near Braunschweig, Germany. Possible stem relatives of caddisflies and moths are known from the Triassic.

tria-067.title: Wrangellia floods the land with basalt
tria-067.text: A belt of lava 2,500 km long now marks one of the Triassic's great eruptions. For about 5 million years, the Wrangellia flood basalts poured onto land and built a large igneous province, a huge pile of volcanic rock. The eruption around 234 million years ago caused abrupt global warming that ended the Ladinian–Carnian cooling. Carbon and osmium isotopes tie it to the Carnian climate upheaval, and seawater osmium shifted at the Ladinian–Carnian boundary. Its rocks belong to the Wrangellia terrane, a crustal fragment later added to western North America.

tria-066.title: The Carnian rains turn Pangaea's deserts green
tria-066.text:
For perhaps 1–2 million years, it rained on Pangaea as never before. Around 234–232 million years ago, in the Carnian pluvial episode, global climate shifted sharply, changing life on land and in the sea. The trigger was volcanic. Eruptions off North America, the Wrangellia large igneous province, set off abrupt global warming that ended the Ladinian–Carnian cooling.

Pangaea's arid climate turned hotter and more humid. Rainfall and runoff surged, and the dry interior became lush forests along rivers. At sea, carbonate platforms, shallow limestone shelves, shrank, and many invertebrates died out, especially ammonoids, bryozoans and crinoids. Yet the same upheaval was a beginning. Early dinosaurs, lepidosaurs and possibly mammaliaforms, mammals and their closest kin, diversified during the event, and coccoliths and dinoflagellates joined the plankton.

tria-068.title: The first true dinosaurs appear
tria-068.text:
Herrerasaurus and Eoraptor were not giants, but they were dinosaurs. The earliest true dinosaurs likely appeared in the Carnian, around the time of the Carnian pluvial episode, and diversified rapidly. Brazil's Santa Maria Formation, radiometrically dated to 233.23 million years ago, and Argentina's Ischigualasto Formation, 231–230 million years old, hold some of the oldest. Nyasasaurus, from Tanzania's Manda Formation, hints that the line may reach back to the Anisian, about 243 million years ago.

Dinosaurs arose from avemetatarsalians, a minor part of Triassic ecosystems. They became dominant only in the Jurassic. Did the rains drive their rise? That is doubtful, because avemetatarsalian diversity grew faster in the Ladinian and Norian than during the wet spell.

tria-069.title: Brazil yields the first sauropodomorphs
tria-069.text: The line that would produce the largest land animals began with small creatures in Brazil. Buriolestes and Saturnalia, from the Santa Maria Formation dated to 233.23 million years ago, are early sauropodomorphs, the dinosaur branch that includes the sauropods. Eoraptor, once grouped with herrerasaurids, now counts as an early sauropodomorph too. Timeline of Earth lists the earliest sauropods at about 233 million years ago, and four-legged sauropodomorphs appeared later in the Late Triassic.

tria-070.title: Ischigualasto's ash and mud bury early dinosaurs
tria-070.text: Volcanic ash helped bury some of the first dinosaurs. The site is a reactivated half-graben, a rift basin tilted along one fault, in northwestern Argentina. There, rivers from volcanic highlands laid down sandstones, mudstones and ash beds up to about 1 km thick. Rain came in strong seasons; one study traces a shift from warm, humid conditions to drier ones around 229.5 million years ago, with partial recovery by 227.8 million. The Ischigualasto Formation is dense with fossils, including Herrerasaurus and Eoraptor among abundant rhynchosaurs and cynodonts.

tria-071.title: Theropods, the meat-eating dinosaurs, arrive
tria-071.text: The lineage that would one day include the great predators began about 231 million years ago. The first theropods, the meat-eating dinosaur line, shared the Carnian with early sauropodomorphs. Their more advanced members, the neotheropods, first appeared later in the Late Triassic.

tria-072.title: Virginia's Cow Branch Formation keeps fish and insects
tria-072.text: Spiders' kin, insects, fish and reptiles share the same rocks in Virginia. The Cow Branch Formation, about 230 million years old, is a Lagerstätte that preserves a wide range of these animals. It gives a rare look at a whole Late Triassic community, small and soft creatures included.

tria-073.title: Madygen yields over 20,000 fossil insects
tria-073.text: More than 20,000 fossil insects have come out of a single formation in Kyrgyzstan. The Madygen Formation, about 230 million years old, is one of the richest Triassic Lagerstätten. Fish, amphibians, reptiles and synapsids, the mammal line, turn up too. Among them is Kyrgyzsaurus, the earliest known drepanosaurid.

tria-074.title: Pterosaurs take to the Triassic skies
tria-074.text: A little after the first true dinosaurs, about 228 million years ago, reptiles took to the air. Pterosaurs, the flying reptiles, sprang from the avemetatarsalians, like dinosaurs a minor part of Triassic ecosystems. Feathers may already have been present in the two groups' common ancestor in the Early Triassic. Early long-tailed pterosaurs appeared in the Norian and quickly spread worldwide. Norian lagoon deposits in northern Italy, such as the Calcare di Zorzino, about 216.6–212 million years old, preserve them beside other reptiles.

tria-075.title: An impact carves Manitoba's Saint Martin crater
tria-075.text: A crater about 40 km across lies in Manitoba, Canada: the Saint Martin structure. Geologists once linked it with Manicouagan and Rochechouart as a single multiple impact. Its age of 227.8 ± 1.1 million years broke that idea, showing the craters formed millions of years apart.

tria-078.title: A disputed end-Carnian crisis drowns a delta
tria-078.text: Repeated floods drowned the vast Boreal Ocean delta plain, shifting shorelines more than 1,000 km and wiping out many of its organisms. Several plant-eating archosauromorph groups died out, and big plant-eating therapsids such as kannemeyeriid dicynodonts dwindled across Laurasia. Coastal habitat loss hit semi-aquatic crurotarsans, the dinosaurs' main rivals, and a reef crisis struck South China. Still, sources hedge on whether this was a distinct extinction, partly because the age of the Carnian–Norian boundary is itself disputed.

tria-081.title: Tuatara relatives spread around the world
tria-081.text: Today the tuatara is a lonely survivor, but its relatives once ranged worldwide. By the end of the Carnian, rhynchocephalians had spread across the globe. They went on to be the dominant small reptiles of the Jurassic.

tria-076.title: Rivers and ash build the colorful Chinle Formation
tria-076.text: The bands of the Painted Desert are a Triassic landscape turned to stone. Rivers, lakes and floodplains, with much volcanic ash, laid down the colorful Chinle Formation across the American Southwest. Exposed there and in Petrified Forest National Park, it holds a unique record of life on land from the late Carnian to the early Norian. U-Pb dating and magnetostratigraphy confirm a Norian age for the lower Chinle.

tria-077.title: Plant-eating dinosaurs spread through the Norian
tria-077.text: Plateosaurus, an early sauropodomorph, evolved around 214 million years ago and roamed Europe, Greenland and North America. It belonged to the plant-eating sauropodomorphs, which diversified in the Norian and began to displace large plant-eating therapsids, perhaps because they coped better with growing aridity. Most Triassic dinosaurs, though, were small predators. Coelophysis, 1–2 m long, was one of the few common ones. Even now, crurotarsan archosaurs, the crocodile line, still filled more ecological niches than dinosaurs did.
